W7220846161.abstract: When autonomous systems take operational authority over urban commerce, accountability and human oversight matter as much as efficiency. We present AAIRM, a governance-aware autonomous retail coordination framework addressing three requirements for trustworthy procurement: tamper-evident decision provenance, data sovereignty, and adaptive demand coordination. AAIRM couples a Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO) ordering policy, a permissioned Blockchain Trust Ledger (BTL) for multi-party audit trails, and a Federated Demand Learning (FDL) layer. Evaluation is simulation-based, using a multi-category synthetic environment and the public M5 dataset; no live retail deployment is claimed. At its cost-optimal operating point (92.3% fill), AAIRM lowers normalized inventory cost by 13.2% (95% CI 12.2-14.2) against a conventionally parameterized reorder-point/economic-order-quantity (ROP-EOQ) baseline and by 10.2% (95% CI 8.0-12.4) on M5. Service parity is obtained by moving AAIRM along its own cost-service frontier rather than by retuning baselines: At 96.1% and 97.4% fill, it retains 8.2-point and 4.9-point advantages. A layered ablation attributes 8.8 points of the advantage to the reinforcement learning (RL) policy and 3.8 points to the combined coordination-and-governance block, which we further decompose into feasibility projection, escalation logic, cross-category policy rules, supplier ranking, and negotiation. The language-model orchestrator contributes 0.6 points (95% CI -0.9 to 2.1), statistically indistinguishable from zero and practically equivalent within a ±2-point margin. Against a feasibility-matched multi-agent RL comparator, the residual cost gap does not survive multiple-comparison correction, so the defensible advantages are hard feasibility and auditability, not cost. The BTL adds 6.6% decision-cycle overhead; its 500-case mutation replay is an integration check, and we give an explicit adversary model showing that crash-fault-tolerant ordering does not resist colluding majorities. FedProx converges within 0.9 WAPE points of centralized training at a 1.3-point cost penalty, without secure aggregation or differential privacy; we analyze rather than evaluate when those mechanisms become necessary. A 500-SKU study exposes a reward-hacking failure in a high-spoilage category, corrected by category-specific governance. We close with an architectural, non-empirical reading of labor exposure and three governance instruments regulators can act on.

W7220932103.abstract: Developing optimization models for production scheduling requires substantial expert effort. Research on large language models (LLMs) has followed two directions: specialized approaches for automated modeling, mostly for mixed-integer linear programming, which often rely on dedicated training or problem-specific architectures that limit industrial deployment; and agentic artificial intelligence for operational decision support, which generally assumes that the optimization model already exists. This study bridges both directions by assessing whether general-purpose LLMs, orchestrated as agents without task-specific training, can formulate and implement constraint programming models from natural-language problem descriptions. Singleagent and multi-agent architectures are integrated with a Model Context Protocol server that provides context-aware retrieval of solver documentation to mitigate hallucinations during implementation. Both are compared with a direct LLM baseline on six industry-oriented problems covering flow-shop, job-shop, flexible job-shop and resource-constrained warehouse scheduling, using three LLMs and assessing modeling accuracy, execution success, latency and token consumption. Formulation proves largely within reach of current LLMs, whereas implementation is the main barrier. The multi-agent workflow raises the share of scripts that run correctly as generated from 14.8% with a direct LLM call to 59.3%, reaching 80.6% on the four less complex problems, while tightly coupled intralogistics models remain an open challenge.

W7220952436.abstract: Manufacturing systems increasingly generate heterogeneous, high-dimensional data, yet many existing artificial intelligence (AI) frameworks remain problem-specific, weakly interpretable, and insufficiently adapted to temporal dependence or material-specific variability. This limits the reliable deployment of AI for process optimization, quality prediction, and future autonomous decision-making in digital manufacturing. To address this gap, this study develops AIMPOD (Artificial Intelligence for Manufacturing Process Optimization and Design), an explainable AI framework that unifies data conditioning, intelligent preprocessing, multi-model learning, ensemble optimization, and interpretability within a single manufacturing-aware workflow.The framework is demonstrated on two distinct case studies: time-aware energy prediction in steel manufacturing and material-aware relative density prediction in laser-beam powder bed fusion of metals (PBF-LB/M). For temporally ordered industrial data, AIMPOD applies leakage-aware chronological validation, while for heterogeneous additive manufacturing data, it adopts material-split modelling to preserve alloy-specific process–structure relationships. Across the steel case, nonlinear and ensemble models achieve test \(R^2\) values between approximately 0.98 and 0.99, while the optimized ensemble reduces RMSE to about 0.63 kWh, improving on the best individual model by roughly 20–25%. In the PBF-LB/M case, pooled materials’ dataset modelling reaches about \(R^2_{\text {test}} \approx 0.76\) , whereas material-specific learning improves performance to about 0.87 for 18Ni300 and 0.78 for CuCrZr. The results demonstrate that AIMPOD enhances predictive robustness while preserving interpretability and providing an adaptive pathway toward explainable and agent-ready manufacturing intelligence.

W7221060324.abstract: LLM tool-use agents operate in dynamic environments where many actions carry operational risk. However, most safety mechanisms react only after errors manifest. Existing pre-emptive approaches either fine-tune the agent on chain-of-thought deliberation or compile natural-language guardrails into runtime checks, but they do so without exposing a structural, auditable verdict. We propose POLAR, a guardrail framework for small tool-calling agents that assesses reversibility through a structured two-layer ontology. POLAR assigns each action a graded reversibility score by deriving a candidate inverse sequence; calls failing a threshold are pruned before execution. Evaluated on $τ^2$-bench across six agent models, POLAR improves mean task reward by 0.11 to 0.18 points on airline for four of six agents, but only eight of eighteen model--domain cells improve overall; retail and stronger agents often regress. POLAR provides an auditable structural check and characterizes its task-utility trade-offs. Reward is not a direct measure of prevented harm.

W7221110404.abstract: A central challenge in enterprise information systems is that the development of generative artificial intelligence has moved from conversational assistants and document generators to autonomous agents that initiate actions․ Agentic architectures have the potential to transform workflows but their probabilistic reasoning is not compatible with transaction integrity‚ security boundaries and governance models that support mission critical enterprise functionality․ This systematic literature review of literature published in 2023-2025 explores four key themes of security and authorization‚ observability and traceability‚ governance and compliance‚ and resilience engineering․ By analyzing the state of the art of 25 peer-reviewed works‚ the review finds that autonomous AI agents are not treated as first-class governed execution entities by existing enterprise architecture frameworks․ We detect four gaps in the literature: a lack of standardized isolation of agent activity‚ a lack of governing models for authorizing agent actions with uncertain outcomes‚ a lack of best practices for tracing the decision chain of the agent's reasoning‚ and a lack of resilience patterns for transactions based on these AI-driven agents․ We conclude by proposing a theoretical research agenda for Agent-Oriented EA․ The review concludes that without discipline‚ organisations risk increased security breaches‚ regulatory non-compliance and systemic operational failures as agentic systems increasingly become the norm.

W7221502991.abstract: Immunosenescence represents a core upstream driver of Alzheimer's disease (AD) and Parkinson's disease (PD), exerting its pathological effects through four mechanistically interconnected cascades: chronic inflammatory imbalance mediated by the senescence-associated secretory phenotype (SASP), oxidative stress arising from immune-metabolic reprogramming, protein homeostasis dysfunction caused by autophagy-lysosomal failure, and disrupted neuro-immune crosstalk secondary to breakdown of central nervous system (CNS) immune privilege. Current clinical practice remains largely constrained to neurotransmitter-based symptomatic management, which can neither arrest upstream pathological progression nor restore lost neuronal populations. Emerging intervention strategies targeting immunosenescence, including senolytic agents, antioxidant and metabolic modulators, autophagy restoration, and precision-targeted nanocarrier delivery, have demonstrated substantial capacity to delay disease progression in preclinical and early clinical investigations. These strategies act through selective clearance of senescent immune cells, remodeling of the neuroinflammatory microenvironment, and restoration of cellular quality-control mechanisms. The multidimensional treatment strategy approaches from the perspectives of artificial intelligence (AI) guided target discovery, nanocarrier engineering, and gut microbiota intervention to simultaneously address multiple nodes in the immunosenescence network, thereby overcoming the inherent limitations of single-target strategies. This review consolidates current mechanistic evidence and translational data to establish immunosenescence as an actionable therapeutic target and to provide a conceptual framework for precision disease-modifying therapy in AD and PD.

W7221530469.abstract: Conspectus Catalytic activity, selectivity, and durability arise from coupled electronic, structural, interfacial, transport, and spin-related processes. Conventional catalyst design has relied largely on electronic effects, strain or stress engineering, active-site construction, and local reaction environment control. Although these strategies have enabled major advances, they do not fully capture the spin degrees of freedom associated with open-shell transition-metal centers and magnetically responsive catalysts. Spin state, spin polarization, magnetic moment, spin density, and magnetic ordering can influence adsorbate binding, transition-state stabilization, charge transfer, and reaction pathways, yet their catalytic consequences are often grouped under the broad label of magnetic enhancement without a clear mechanistic assignment. In this Account, we develop explicit spin regulation as a framework for magnetism-informed catalysis. Magnetic enhancement describes an observed response to a magnetic field, a magnetic component, or a magnetic environment. Explicit spin regulation, by contrast, requires deliberate modulation of spin-related variables at or near catalytically active sites and a mechanistic connection to catalytic function. We organize this framework around two routes. Catalyst-integrated spin levers use promoters, interfaces, or interphases to tune the active-site spin/electronic structure, whereas field-induced spin levers introduce external fields or catalyst-localized magnetic perturbations during catalysis. Although implemented differently, both routes seek to control how the active-site spin governs adsorption, transition-state energetics, charge transfer, selectivity, stability, and durability. Our studies provide representative evidence for this framework. Promoter-induced spin modulation stabilizes the N–N dissociation transition state beyond conventional electrostatic promotion, establishing the spin-promotion effect as a catalyst-integrated design principle. In electrocatalysis, external fields, embedded nanomagnets, and magnetic proximity effects provide progressively localized perturbations that can be connected to spin-sensitive active sites, key intermediates, or local magnetic ordering. These examples also show why performance enhancement alone is insufficient. A convincing assignment should connect the imposed perturbation, the active-site spin/electronic response, the affected intermediate or transition state, and the resulting catalytic consequence. Magnetic measurements, electron paramagnetic resonance spectroscopy, element-specific X-ray spectroscopies, operando methods, kinetic analysis, and spin-polarized theory provide complementary elements of this evidence loop. Building on this mechanistic framework, we further translate the active-site spin into catalyst-design descriptors. The local metal-center spin moment can be correlated with oxygen-intermediate adsorption and activity trends, enabling descriptor-guided screening of dual-atom catalysts. Spin-related variables may also inform stability and durability through their connections to phase stability, surface reconstruction, active-site preservation, dissolution resistance, and long-term operation. Generalizing these insights requires paired, standardized, and machine-readable datasets that connect magnetic perturbations, active-site structures, spin-sensitive measurements, catalytic metrics, and durability under comparable conditions. Artificial intelligence-assisted literature mining, knowledge graph construction, high-throughput spin-polarized calculations, active learning, and magnetism-aware machine-learning interatomic potentials may help identify transferable spin descriptors and extend spin-regulated catalyst design to dynamic interfaces. The broader aim is to move magnetism-informed catalysis from phenomenological enhancement toward predictive control through deliberate regulation of the active-site spin.

W7221590923.abstract: Enterprise artificial intelligence (AI) is moving from isolated predictive models and conversational assistants toward agentic systems that plan, use tools, collaborate, and act within delegated authority. This shift opens a governance gap, because organizations deploy AI agents faster than they establish oversight, decision authority, auditability, and value assurance. This study develops the Artificial Intelligence Control Tower (AICT), a governance-driven enterprise operating model for orchestrating and assuring autonomous business decision-making. Design Science Research is used to synthesize evidence from enterprise AI, multi-agent systems, decision intelligence, and responsible AI, together with the NIST AI Risk Management Framework, ISO/IEC 42001, ISO/IEC 23894, the OECD AI Principles, and the European Union Artificial Intelligence Act. The resulting artifact comprises six integrated layers: enterprise data and knowledge foundation, AI workforce and agent registry, orchestration and workflow control, decision assurance, governance and compliance, and executive value oversight. Its control logic is formalized through nine equations that express aggregated assurance confidence, decision risk, autonomy-tier assignment, policy admissibility, execution authority, the expected net value of delegated autonomy, governance coverage, and a weighted maturity index. The framework further specifies an eight-stage decision lifecycle, four risk-tiered autonomy levels, a five-level maturity model, and a balanced performance system covering operational, financial, quality, governance, risk, and workforce outcomes. Ex ante evaluation against eight design criteria and five enterprise scenarios (procurement, inventory, workforce planning, operational risk, and executive performance) indicates that AICT can improve decision velocity and traceability while limiting authority drift and unmanaged automation. The study contributes a unifying enterprise architecture, a formal decision-governance model, seven testable propositions, an implementation roadmap, and a measurement agenda, with relevance to Saudi Vision 2030 organizations that are scaling AI under national and international governance expectations.

W7221802692.abstract: Benchmarks report what an Artificial Intelligence (AI) agent can do on a task suite, but not whether one released version has been engineered with the controls that make it reliable, safe and observable, or how strongly that is shown. This paper proposes AgentStripes, an evidence-graded maturity model for AI agents. It defines levels (0 to 7 stripes), process areas (12 areas holding 40 capabilities), three gates (basic, safety, proof) that hold an agent at a level however high its score, and evidence grades E0 to E5. Each applicable capability receives a rating from 0 to 3 and a separate evidence level; these are combined into a credit, aggregated into a severity-weighted score and converted into stripes that the gates limit. Instruments gather evidence, language-model judges interpret it under explicit criteria, and the arithmetic is deterministic. The model is compared with standards at topic level without a claim of conformance, and an unexecuted validation protocol is specified. An empirical evaluation (exploratory, non-confirmatory) of 30 public Python agent repositories, with static evidence only, is a demonstration and not a validation: static evidence caps every final stripe at 2, 26 repositories end at one stripe and 4 at two, and this distinction is unreliable, since re-judging changed the final stripe of 4 of 22 repositories (engine, dossier and panel changed), whereas none of 8 panel-only repeats, all at stripe 1, changed. The parameters are expert conventions without outcome based calibration, and the stripes have not been shown to predict reliability or safety.

W7221831210.abstract: Spiking neural networks target energy-efficient language modeling through sparse, binary activations, but the efficiency-accuracy tradeoff of spiking language models is uncharacterized at scale. We present the first Chinchilla-style IsoFLOP scaling study of a spiking language model, sweeping SpikeGPT-family models (RWKV backbone) from width 384 to 1536 across compute budgets from $3\times10^{17}$ to $10^{19}$ FLOPs on FineWeb-EDU. We report two findings. First, the compute-optimal frontier is $N_{opt} \propto C^{0.56}$, close to the 0.50 that Hoffmann et al. report for dense Transformers, so spiking does not change how parameters and data should be traded off under a compute budget. Second, against non-spiking RWKV and Transformer baselines trained the same way, the loss gap splits into a backbone cost of about 0.16 nats that does not change with compute and a spiking cost that falls steadily with compute, from 0.34 to 0.23 nats over our range. These results give the first compute-optimal recipe for spiking language models and quantify the accuracy cost of their sparsity.

W7221836176.abstract: Massive mechanical oscillators couple directly to forces, accelerations and gravity, making them attractive probes of new physics and of quantum mechanics at macroscopic scales. Pushing sensitivities beyond the standard quantum limit for signals of unknown phase requires non-Gaussian quantum states, whose metrological advantage has so far been confined to lighter systems such as trapped ions. Here we operate a microgram-scale acoustic mode of a high-overtone bulk acoustic wave resonator as a phase-insensitive quantum-enhanced sensor. A transmon qubit prepares the mode in Fock states of up to seven phonons by optimal control, and resolves its phonon-number distribution after interaction with a weak resonant signal. Bayesian analysis yields a Fisher information five times the vacuum value, a 7.0 dB gain in signal-amplitude sensitivity over any classical probe state, irrespective of its energy, currently limited by state preparation infidelities. We then train a neural network on the measured sensor response to perform Bayesian estimation without any analytical model of the system, showing the same sensitivity gain with half the systematic bias. Our results establish acoustic resonators prepared in non-Gaussian states as quantum-enhanced probes for high-frequency gravitational waves, dark matter and wave-function collapse.

W7222453271.abstract: Enterprise adoption of generative AI is moving from conversational assistants toward autonomous agents capable of reading enterprise data, invoking business logic, and performing operational actions. In a Salesforce environment, this evolution creates a security problem that differs materially from conventional API integration: an AI agent can interpret natural-language intent, select tools dynamically, construct parameters, and execute multi-step workflows, while the underlying CRM contains highly sensitive customer, financial, and operational information. Model Context Protocol (MCP) provides a standardized interaction layer between AI applications and external capabilities, but protocol-level connectivity does not by itself solve identity, authorization, data minimization, action governance, or audit requirements. This paper proposes a security-oriented reference architecture for enterprise AI agents interacting with Salesforce through MCP. The architecture combines per-user authentication, least-privilege authorization, Salesforce-native object and field controls, tool-level governance, context minimization, human approval for high-impact actions, continuous audit, and a five-factor risk model covering data impact, security impact, automation impact, integration impact, and reversibility. The paper maps these controls to current Salesforce Hosted MCP security capabilities and contemporary AI security guidance, then defines a practical evaluation framework for testing confidentiality, integrity, authorization correctness, prompt-injection resilience, operational safety, and auditability. The contribution is a reusable architectural pattern for enterprises that want to expose Salesforce capabilities to agentic AI without replacing established CRM governance with an opaque AI-specific security layer.

W7222839128.abstract: Background: Autonomous LLM agents increasingly operate in shared environments where behavior depends on interaction history, role allocation, local norms, authority, and group structure. Objective: This conceptual methods paper develops a psychometric operationalization of dynamic functional roles in autonomous multi-agent systems using PersonaMatrix-derived measurement principles without attributing human psychological ontology to AI. Methods: A targeted evidence synthesis (2019–2026) was conducted across AI psychometrics, dynamic multi-agent roles, collective-field modeling, norm emergence, trajectory prediction, and anthropomorphism. Peer-reviewed sources were prioritized, while current OpenAI, METR/Redwood, Anthropic, and Moltbook materials were used as primary or emerging evidence for recent agent ecosystems. Results: The framework separates output-level stability (RSI, IDS, RCS) from role-level and field-level constructs. It proposes the Functional Role Consistency Index, Role Transition Index, Agent–Field Differentiation Index, Collective Utility Index, Norm Conflict Index, Regulatory Closure Index, and Field Role Composition Vector. Three falsifiable hypotheses test whether role variables add out-of-sample predictive value for agent behavior, role transitions, and future field states. Conclusion: PersonaMatrix is positioned as a measurement architecture rather than an AI personality diagnosis. The archetypal-role hypothesis is supported only if role coding is reliable, improves prediction beyond non-archetypal baselines, and generalizes to unseen agents and independent multi-agent environments.

W7222959596.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used to automate AI research, including language-model (LM) development, offering a potential path toward recursive self-improvement. However, turning experimental feedback into a learned ability to propose effective improvements across models faces two challenges. First, training such an ability with real feedback is expensive: reinforcement learning (RL) requires evaluating tens of thousands of proposals, each potentially requiring a full model-training run. Even at ten GPU-hours per run, reward collection alone would consume hundreds of thousands of GPU-hours, motivating a cheaper surrogate. Second, surrogate feedback can become unreliable as policy optimization favors overestimated proposals when the proposal distribution shifts. To address these challenges, we propose LM2LM, which trains LLMs with RL to generate effective LM improvement proposals. To provide scalable feedback, we use a research world model (RWM), a frozen LLM that predicts proposal gains from real experimental records provided in context, as the reward model for RL. To maintain feedback reliability, we periodically execute current-policy proposals ranked highly by the RWM and add their measured outcomes to its context. Across eight autoregressive and diffusion LM development environments, real-execution evaluations on held-out tasks show that LM2LM enables Qwen3.8-27B to outperform GPT-6-sol, even when GPT-6-sol is given 300 real experimental records in context, while requiring 33% lower data-generation cost. LM2LM also generalizes to a model family unseen during training.

W7223003364.abstract: Distributed networks have become increasingly complex and as such face the continuing challenge of strong defense against attacks on these networks with a strong Cyber Defense or Cyber Security presence. Traditional centralized Intrusion Detection Systems (IDS) have scalability difficulties, response times that are very slow, and limited capabilities to adapt and respond dynamically to new and evolving threats from Cyber-Attackers. To overcome these issues and to provide a coop-based Cyber Defense framework, this paper describes the design, architecture, and operation of an autonomous independent multi-agent Artificial Intelligence (AI) framework for Cyber Defense; this Cyber Defense will have no single point of failure. The decentralized agents that will comprise the proposed Cyber Defense system will use Reinforcement Learning (RL) during execution, allowing them to detect and to mitigate threats in an adaptive and real-time manner. Each individual agent independently operates while still exchanging threat intelligence with neighboring agents thereby improving the overall global situational awareness and coordinated response to threats from adversaries that utilizes this information for malicious purposes. The experimental evaluation using benchmark datasets shows that the proposed methodology provides a detection accuracy of 94.8%, which exceeds both centralized intrusion detection systems (85.2%) and traditional machine learning based models (88.6%). Additionally, the proposed methodology reduces false positives to 5.1% versus 12.5% using traditional methods and improves response times by approximately 25-40%. Scalability analysis demonstrates that as the number of agents increases, performance increases as well, indicating the effectiveness of decentralized cooperation within the overall framework. These results demonstrate that the proposed multi-agent framework provides a safe and scalable means of responding to the threats posed by adversaries to next-generation cyber defense mechanisms deployed across distributed networks.

W7223075994.abstract: Post hoc explanation methods describe how a model’s output co-varies with its inputs, which is not the same as how the world responds to a change. This paper examines causal machine learning as a foundation for explainable and interpretable AI. It reviews the limits of associational attribution, surveys methods for causal discovery, effect estimation, counterfactual generation and causal attribution, and proposes CausalXAI, a modular pipeline that connects them. In a controlled simulation with known ground truth, standard permutation importance and Shapley-style attributions placed 29–41% of their importance on a feature with no causal effect, whereas the causal pipeline placed none, and its effect-estimation error was 0.027 against 0.54 at 2,000 training samples. Under a shift in the spurious feature’s behaviour, the causal-parent model held a constant error while the all-feature model’s error rose 2.7-fold. We discuss assumptions, limitations and ethical considerations.

W7223131049.abstract: Abstract Matched filtering provides the foundation for gravitational-wave detection, with waveform similarity traditionally described through the local geometry of the template-space metric. We investigate whether the exact pairwise matched-filter mismatch (PMM) over a finite waveform bank can instead be used to learn a global coordinate system for gravitational-wave templates. As a controlled proof of concept, we consider finite banks of nonspinning IMRPhenomD binary-black-hole waveforms over a fixed component-mass range. We formulate this as a supervised representation-learning problem in which physically computed PMM provides the supervision signal, and train a neural network so that Euclidean distances between latent coordinates approximate the mismatch between waveform pairs. Across waveform banks containing up to 8192 templates, the learned representation preserves both global pairwise mismatch relationships and local matched-filter neighborhoods while consistently outperforming Euclidean retrieval in the physical coordinate systems considered. Comparison with Classical Multidimensional Scaling shows that the learned encoder provides a competitive low-dimensional approximation of the finite-bank mismatch geometry while simultaneously learning an explicit mapping applicable to previously unseen waveforms. For previously unseen query waveforms drawn from the same waveform family and parameter distribution, the learned representation recovers the exhaustive best-matching template for 99.02% of queries using only 10 candidate templates from an 8192-template bank and for all queries using 20 candidates, reducing the number of exact matched-filter evaluations by factors of 819.2 and 409.6, respectively. Within this controlled setting, these results demonstrate that PMM provides an effective supervision signal for learning global geometric representations of waveform similarity and establish a proof of concept for mismatch-supervised organization and candidate retrieval in finite waveform banks.

W7223134759.abstract: The mechanisms of governance are critical in enabling responsible AI that can assist in compliance, transparency, accountability and continual risk monitoring. Traditional governance practices were more likely to cover these aspects individually and hence were not as effective in providing assurance for the lifecycle. This work suggested an Adaptive Transparent AI Governance Framework (ATAGF), which fuses together a Governance Evidence Hypergraph, Policy-Trace Alignment Mechanism, Sociotechnical Transparency Index, Accountability Propagation Matrix, Adaptive Governance Decision Engine and a Governance Drift Detector. The framework has been applied to build an archive of governance evidence, and to link up these pieces of evidence and evaluate how aligned policies are in terms of transparency, accountability, governance quality and type of policy linkages. Experimental testing over ten simulated scenarios of AI governance showed maximum policy alignment of 97.9%, transparency of 97.0%, accountability of 97.5% and overall Trustworthy Governance Score of 97.7%. The integrated framework was assessed with regards to the individual approaches of regulatory, governance and transparency and the integrated framework showed the best governance performance. The framework therefore provided the evidence-based and transparent governance of AI, and could adapt based on the changing policies, risks, and stakeholder needs. Future enhancements of ATAGF will involve the use of actual organizational data, regulations, cross domain applications of AI, and automated compliance monitoring for additional validation, further development of practical deployment, and generalization.

W7223140337.abstract: Security operations centers increasingly rely on agentic artificial intelligence systems, which combine large language model reasoning with tool invocation and multi-step planning, to automate alert triage, investigation, and response. Independent research groups have proposed structurally distinct architectures for this purpose, ranging from single-agent reasoning loops to multi-agent systems with shared context or deterministic safety constraints, but no publication has systematically compared these designs against a common set of criteria. This review addresses that gap by constructing a five-dimension classification framework covering agent cardinality, coordination mechanism, autonomy boundary, safety enforcement layer, and validation maturity. A corpus of published systems relevant to security operations was retrieved from academic preprint archives and conference proceedings and coded against this framework. Five recurring design patterns were identified, together with the available quantitative evidence comparing them, including a controlled trial showing that multi-agent orchestration produced consistently reliable recommendations while single-agent approaches did not. The analysis found that claimed autonomy consistently outpaced empirical validation across the reviewed designs, with most systems evaluated no further than a single organizational deployment despite permitting autonomous action. These findings indicate that validation maturity should be assessed independently from architectural sophistication when organizations evaluate agentic artificial intelligence for security operations, and they identify calibration and human oversight effectiveness as priority areas for future empirical study.

W7223151762.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have significantly advanced natural language processing and artificial intelligence applications through their capabilities in reasoning, text generation and knowledge retrieval. However, LLMs are still vulnerable to two important challenges: hallucination, generating factually incorrect or fabricated content, and response deviation, meaning systematic deviations from ground-truth responses. These limitations raise serious concerns regarding reliability and trustworthiness in academic and research environments. This study offers a thorough comparative analysis using a variety of metrics of ten advanced LLMs ChatGPT, Gemini, Claude~3.5~Sonnet, LLaMA~3, Mistral, Grok, Perplexity, DeepSeek~V3, Falcon, and Gemma based on a benchmark consisting of 70 carefully designed academic prompts across four complexity levels: Basic, Explanation, Advanced, and Tricky, evaluated in February 2025 on specific model versions. Each response was independently evaluated by three reviewers using five metrics: Accuracy, Precision, Recall, Response Deviation Index, and Hallucination Index. Perplexity and DeepSeek~V3 achieved the highest overall accuracy, while Gemini demonstrated strong recall and a well-balanced performance profile across all five metrics. LLaMA~3 showed strong resistance against hallucinations through a conservative method of generation. Advanced-level prompts proved most challenging across all models, while Tricky prompts were handled more reliably owing to their binary true/false structure. Falcon achieved perfect precision and zero hallucinations, but at the cost of the lowest recall and the highest response deviation. The results show a fundamental trade-off between response completeness and factual reliability, intensified by prompt complexity.

W7223338039.abstract: Melting point prediction plays a pivotal role in chemistry, materials science, and pharmaceuticals, where it informs compound identification, purity assessment, and design of thermally robust materials. Despite advances in computational modeling, current methods face challenges in accuracy, interpretability, and computational efficiency, largely due to limited experimental datasets and the nonlinear, discontinuous relationship between molecular structure and melting behavior. In this study, we curate a harmonized dataset of 117 752 unique organic crystals by integrating and standardizing multiple public sources, emphasizing reproducibility and molecular uniqueness. We systematically evaluate classical machine learning models using molecular embeddings derived from SMILES strings, including ChemBERTa, MoLFormer, Morgan fingerprints, and Uni-Mol, and compare them with advanced graph neural network (GNN) architectures such as our custom implementation and the widely used Chemprop framework. Our analysis demonstrates that gradient-boosted tree models offer notable computational efficiency, while GNNs and transformer-based models like MoLFormer provide superior predictive accuracy, particularly when enhanced with attention mechanisms. By integrating ChemBERTa and MoLFormer embeddings in the TabM model, we achieve a mean absolute error (MAE) of 26.75 K and an RMSE of 35.36 K, surpassing individual model performance. These results highlight the benefits of hybrid modeling strategies that balance interpretability, scalability, and accuracy, offering a robust framework for accelerating materials discovery and pharmaceutical development through improved melting point prediction. Nevertheless, Chemprop exhibits considerably higher accuracy but demands approximately five times greater resources during training.

W7223349864.abstract: Abstract Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly deployed as agents that plan, remember, call tools, coordinate with other agents and act over long horizons with limited supervision. Evidence on whether such agents work reliably is scattered and sometimes contradictory, and recent reviews largely describe architectures, benchmarks or threats in isolation. This systematic, taxonomy-driven critical review follows PRISMA 2020 reporting where applicable, without meta-analytic pooling, and synthesises 98 verified sources published up to 30 June 2026. It differs from prior reviews in four ways. First, it weighs evidence: eight headline claims are graded by an explicit rule, and contradictions are traced to moderators such as feedback source, equal-compute comparison and task verifiability. Second, it specifies a closed-loop reference framework operationally, adding a verification stage and a safety-and-authorisation gate, and codes ten published systems against it; none fully implements both control stages. Third, it links capabilities to evaluation hooks, readiness levels and re-assurance triggers for agents that change after deployment. Fourth, its evidence base is auditable through re-executed searches with measured recall, verified references and a released evidence matrix. High-confidence findings are that intrinsic self-correction is unreliable, long-horizon autonomous planning remains weak and tool-using agents are broadly vulnerable to injection. Multi-agent benefits are conditional (moderate confidence), whereas claims about benchmark validity and memory consistency rest mainly on preprints. A reliability model quantifies the value of independent verification, and an eighteen-direction roadmap is ranked by an explicit priority rule.

W7223404996.abstract: AI agents that operate external tools can continue acting after a user narrows their permissions, creating a security problem that final-state evaluation may fail to detect. Existing agent benchmarks commonly emphasize task completion or resulting state, but those outcomes do not reveal whether an unauthorized operation was proposed, approved, dispatched, or merely prevented by a downstream error. We investigate permission withdrawal as a trajectory-level authorization problem and evaluate whether runtime gates can preserve revised permissions while allowing agents to complete work that remains authorized. Two acting models were tested in a deterministic tool environment under prompt-only execution, a rule-based reference gate, and a model-based gate. A 72-episode diagnostic examined two previously exposed write workflows, followed by a separately frozen 384-episode extension spanning eight new tasks and four authorization mechanisms. In the diagnostic, prompt-only agents executed forbidden same-value writes in two episodes; both runtime gates prevented forbidden execution, although the model gate falsely rejected three authorized calls. In the extension, 346 of 384 episodes completed safely and 383 preserved the required protected state. No forbidden request executed successfully, yet the model gate approved three unauthorized requests that were stopped only because the referenced resources did not exist. The results demonstrate that correct final state and zero forbidden execution can still conceal failures in authorization reasoning. We contribute a replayable evaluation framework that separates proposals, gate decisions, dispatch, state transitions, and useful completion, enabling more precise assessment of security controls for tool-using agents.

W7223413137.abstract: The increasing release and reuse of Large Language Models (LLMs) as open-weight checkpoints make model fingerprinting important for ownership protection and offline auditing. Existing fingerprinting methods typically construct evidence from query responses, generated outputs, or input-induced activations. Although effective in representation-based settings, they can be affected by prompt selection, decoding configuration, inference environment, and forward-pass implementation, which may limit their applicability. Here we introduce a model-intrinsic weight-level framework that derives compact fingerprints from spectral structures encoded in LLM parameters. Specifically, the framework constructs GATE spectral scalar features from the singular-value distributions of GATE projection weights in gated feed-forward networks (FFNs), and aggregates the resulting layer-wise features through depth-wise segmented pooling to form a model-level fingerprint. Such representation preserves coarse layer-depth organization while reducing dependence on strict layer-to-layer alignment, enabling comparison across LLMs with different depths. The similarity between fingerprints is computed by linear centered kernel alignment. The entire pipeline is training-free and does not require input samples, generated outputs, forward activations, or an auxiliary verifier. Experiments on representative LLM families and post-training variants have demonstrated a clear separation between source-related models and unrelated ones, and stable similarity under instruction tuning, quantization, pruning, and distillation-related modifications, which verify that spectral features are robust evidence for LLM fingerprinting.

W7223468338.abstract: High-precision knowledge retrieval within specialized scientific infrastructures, such as CERN's large-scale data ecosystem, presents unique challenges for standard Large Language Models (LLMs). Conventional Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) frameworks often suffer from structural fragmentation and inadequate retrieval of technical identifiers. This paper proposes an optimized RAG framework utilizing a Hybrid Similarity Scoring mechanism that integrates BM25 lexical matching with dense semantic retrieval. The methodology focuses on enhancing technical factuality through a neural re-ranking pipeline and instruction-formatted system prompting. Extensive experiments were conducted to evaluate three distinct chunking strategies and the influence of various LLM hyperparameters on model grounding. Results indicate that the proposed framework achieves a 2–8% improvement in retrieval relevance and a 2% reduction in hallucinations compared to standard RAG baselines, providing a robust solution for complex technical domain interaction.

W7223573812.abstract: The indirect detection of dark matter through gamma-ray emission from dwarf spheroidal galaxies (dSphs) provides a promising avenue for probing the particle nature of dark matter. However, extracting dark matter parameters from gamma-ray spectra remains a challenging inverse problem, particularly when conventional statistical and computational methods require repeated evaluations of physical models over a large parameter space. In this study, we develop a Physics-Informed Neural Network (PINN) in an inverse configuration to infer key dark matter properties, including the particle mass and velocity-averaged annihilation cross section, from gamma-ray spectral data associated with dSphs. The proposed framework incorporates the underlying dark matter annihilation flux equation directly into the learning process, allowing the network to exploit both observational information and physical constraints. This physics-informed formulation enables the model to establish a physically consistent mapping between gamma-ray spectra and the corresponding dark matter parameters. The proposed PINN achieves a low spectral reconstruction error, with a Mean Squared Error (MSE) of 1.7×10-3, while providing a computationally efficient alternative to conventional parameter-inference approaches. These results demonstrate the potential of PINNs for accelerating inverse dark matter analyses and establishing efficient surrogate models for gamma-ray-based indirect detection. The framework provides a foundation for extending physics-informed machine learning to more realistic observational datasets and broader dark matter parameter spaces.

W7223681059.abstract: Galactic thermal dust emission is the dominant foreground contaminant of the cosmic microwave background (CMB) at frequencies above 100 GHz, and its accurate separation is essential for current and future CMB experiments. Deep learning methods, in particular convolutional architectures such as the U-Net, have demonstrated strong performance for CMB component separation, but typically operate as purely data-driven models with no explicit enforcement of the physical laws governing the emission they reconstruct. In this work, we present a Physics-Informed Neural Network (PINN) that embeds the Modified Black Body (MBB) spectral model as a hard, differentiable architectural constraint, and we compare it against a standard U-Net baseline trained under an identical pipeline. Both architectures are trained on realistic simulated Planck HFI patches at four frequencies (143, 217, 353 and 545 GHz) and evaluated on a shared validation set as well as on three independent Galactic dust realizations from the PySM phenomenological dust models named D4, D7 and D10. We find that both networks achieve comparable reconstruction quality across all evaluated datasets, with a Structural Similarity Index Measure consistently above 0.96 and a fitted angular power-spectrum spectral index that agrees with the input to within 1% in every region. Embedding the physical constraint in the PINN does not measurably degrade reconstruction accuracy relative to the unconstrained U-Net, while additionally guaranteeing that every predicted output corresponds to a thermodynamically admissible physical configuration. These results establish the physics-informed formulation as a viable methodological alternative for dust component separation, providing physical interpretability without a trade-off in reconstruction fidelity.

W7223975169.abstract: AI agents are increasingly proposed as autonomous experimenters, yet the benchmarks that test them mostly offer cheap experiments that answer at once. Experiments in physical facilities are different: they take months, occupy scarce equipment and cannot be undone. We present SlowLab, a benchmark in which an agent runs a one-year campaign in four simulated greenhouse compartments on a site whose crop, facility and prices are hidden. The agent decides when to plant which climate policy, whether to stop a crop and which measurements to read while crops grow, and at the end recommends one policy, which a private evaluator scores in weather the agent never saw. In a preregistered study on 48 unseen sites, three low-cost language-model agents ended near a standard grower setting and clearly below a Bayesian-optimisation baseline that starts from that setting. They ran the facility as two synchronous batches, so measurements taken during the season never changed what they planted, and these measurements improved no method's result. Letting other methods re-read the evidence a campaign had collected did not yield significantly better recommendations, which points to where the models start and which experiments they try. Code is released under the MIT license.

W7224085398.abstract: Acute myeloid leukemia (AML) with IDH1 mutations is amenable to targeted therapy, highlighting the need for reliable identification. We developed an attention-based multiple-instance learning model to predict IDH1 mutation status using bone marrow smear whole-slide images from 436 AML patients across four centers in Germany and the US, achieving a mean single pooled ROC-AUC of 0.81. In top tile analysis, model predictions for IDH1 were associated with immature leukemia phenotypes.

W7224116134.abstract: Multi-Agent Systems (MAS) offer an effective approach for solving complex and large-scale problems in distributed artificial intelligence by dividing them into smaller subtasks handled by multiple autonomous agents. Each agent can perceive its environment, process information, make decisions, and perform actions according to its assigned objectives. Agents communicate, collaborate, and coordinate to achieve individual and collective goals, providing advantages such as scalability, adaptability, flexibility, robustness, and fault tolerance. The proposed Multi-Agent Task Automation System uses heterogeneous agents dynamically assigned tasks according to their capabilities, resource availability, current workload, task priority, execution cost, and contextual relevance. A mediator-based coordination mechanism supports agent discovery and task routing while allowing direct peer-to-peer communication when necessary. Dynamic task allocation and load balancing help distribute work efficiently. Reinforcement learning can enhance agent decision-making by allowing agents to learn from feedback and improve their strategies over time. The system also incorporates fault detection, recovery, authentication, secure communication, and trust evaluation to improve reliability and security. The implementation uses Python, AutoGen, large language models, APIs, and external tools, with structured message passing enabling agents to interact and execute tasks collaboratively. Tasks are initiated through user input and processed using iterative communication, reasoning, and tool execution. The proposed approach demonstrates the potential of MAS to improve task execution efficiency, response time, resource utilization, adaptability, scalability, and fault tolerance compared with traditional centralized approaches. However, communication overhead, coordination complexity, security risks, synchronization, and efficient task allocation remain important challenges.

W7224273046.abstract: Generative adversarial distillation (GAD) provides on-policy feedback for black-box distillation by training a discriminator that ranks teacher and student responses to the same prompt.While effective, GAD is also costly: every step pays for a discriminator update, an actor update over the full response, and the indirect cost of recovering whenever the discriminator and the actor progress at incompatible rates.We argue that the right way to make GAD efficient is not to make individual updates cheaper but to decide when each update is worth its cost.To this end, we introduce curriculumefficient GAD (CE-GAD), an adaptive recipe that monitors a small set of training signals and uses them to (i) skip discriminator updates that would not change the reward, (ii) constrain actor updates and prune per-token gradients to the subset that actually carries signal, and (iii) rescale rewards and normalize advantages to preserve within-batch contrast under saturation.Evaluations across four models from two open-source families (Qwen2.5 at 3B/7B/14B and Llama-3.2-3B)demonstrate that CE-GAD matches or surpasses vanilla GAD on quality while winning on 12 out of 16 individual benchmark configurations.Specifically, on Qwen2.5-7B,CE-GAD improves the average score by up to +3% relative compared to the base model, while reducing per-step wall-clock time by up to 8× relative to vanilla GAD.

W7224276023.abstract: Cost-effective deployment of large language models (LLMs) often relies on routing each query to either a low-cost local model or a stronger expert model.Existing routers typically decide either before generation, which is cheap but cannot observe the local model's answer, or after generation, which provides a stronger correctness signal but incurs additional generation cost.We argue that this dichotomy overlooks a third option: treating local generation itself as an optional informationacquisition action.To this end, we propose Generation-Gated Cascaded Routing for Large Language Models (GenGate), a lightweight fine-tuning method that trains a local LLM to internalize cascaded routing decisions while preserving its generation capability.A Bellman-motivated prior gate first decides whether to generate a local attempt.If an attempt is produced, a correctness-supervised posterior gate then decides whether to submit it or defer to the expert model.Both decisions are expressed through action-token probabilities in the same model, requiring no external router or auxiliary classifier at inference time.Compared with routers that decide strictly before or after local generation, Gen-Gate reduces joint deployment cost while maintaining competitive routing accuracy across task domains, preserving the benefits of posterior routing without requiring local generation for every query.Code is available at https://github.com/xsyhh/GenGate.

W7224751520.abstract: The acceleration of the regulatory requirement, globalization of operations and digital transformation has increased the corporate vulnerability to legal risk. The current legal risk management methods which are mostly reactive and manual fail to handle the scale and complexity of the modern legal and compliance issues. Corporations are in turn moving towards artificial intelligence (AI) more and more as a method of improving legal risk identification, evaluation, and reduction. The paper explores the ways of using AI to balance the control of corporate legal risk and governance, accountability, and ethical responsibility. Using a qualitative and conceptual research of the existing literature, the study examines the major types of corporate legal risk such as regulatory compliance, contractual risk, litigation exposure, governance failures, and data protection issues. The paper examines AI applications within the corporate legal functions, including natural language processing, machine learning, and predictive analytics, and puts into the limelight, how these applications can be used to facilitate proactive and predictive risk management. Meanwhile, the paper critically considers the issues related to the use of AI such as algorithmic bias, transparency, threats to privacy, and legal accountability ambiguity. To resolve the challenges a conceptual framework is suggested, which incorporates the AI capabilities in the corporate level of legal risk management in a regulation-focused and ethically sound framework. The article adds to the literature because it offers a comprehensive view of AI-sensitive law risk management and offers useful data that corporations should consider in terms of finding the balance between innovation and legal accountability.

W7224836594.abstract: Pulmonary arterial hypertension (PAH) is a progressive vascular disorder characterized by elevated pulmonary vascular resistance and right ventricular dysfunction. Conventional imaging modalities, chest computed tomography (CT) and cardiac ultrasound (echocardiography), provide complementary structural and functional information but exhibit incomplete sensitivity and specificity when used alone. This study aimed to evaluate a multimodal artificial intelligence (AI) model integrating chest CT and cardiac ultrasound for auxiliary PAH diagnosis, benchmarked against right heart catheterization (RHC) as the reference standard. A retrospective observational study was conducted on 100 patients (mean age 52.6 ± 15.2 years; 56% female) with suspected PAH between January 2020 and December 2024. Each underwent high-resolution chest CT, transthoracic echocardiography, and RHC within a 2-week interval. Imaging-derived structural and functional features were integrated within an attention-based multimodal AI framework. Diagnostic metrics were calculated for chest CT, cardiac ultrasound, and multimodal AI against the archived RHC clinical classification. The multimodal AI system achieved sensitivity of 92.2%, specificity of 88.9%, accuracy of 91.0%, and AUC of 0.930, compared with CT (sensitivity 84.4%, specificity 80.6%, accuracy 83.0%, AUC 0.860) and echocardiography (sensitivity 79.7%, specificity 77.8%, accuracy 79.0%, AUC 0.840). McNemar tests of paired binary classifications favored AI over CT (p = 0.0078) and echocardiography (p = 0.00049). Exploratory subgroup analyses were performed for borderline pulmonary artery diameter and connective tissue disease. The multimodal approach showed improved overall discrimination in this internal retrospective evaluation and should be considered an auxiliary, noninvasive tool that requires external prospective validation.

W7224875557.abstract: This article examines agentic artificial intelligence as an emerging class of technologies that fundamentally reshapes business process automation, shifting the paradigm from reactive assistant systems to autonomous solutions capable of independent planning, decision-making, and execution of multi-step actions within defined authority boundaries. The aim of this study stems from a growing realization that traditional AI implementation strategies are failing to deliver expected returns. This discrepancy between strategic ambitions and practical outcomes calls for a systematic investigation of alternative approaches to AI integration, particularly those offering higher autonomy and operational transformation potential. The study demonstrates that agentic AI fundamentally transforms the cost structure of business operations by converting variable labor expenses into predominantly fixed and highly scalable technology costs, thereby altering the economics of enterprise operations. The analysis reveals that organizations implementing agentic AI achieve dramatic operational improvements including task completion time reductions and significant cost optimizations through the elimination of manual inefficiencies. The findings further show that successful scaling of agentic systems depends not so much on technological excellence as on organizational readiness, in particular the development of appropriate governance frameworks for managing autonomous systems, ensuring transparency and explainability in automated decision-making, and integrating AI agents effectively into hybrid human-machine teams while addressing workforce skill gaps. The practical value of this research lies in providing business leaders and technology managers with actionable insights for strategic decision-making regarding AI investments, offering a systematic framework for evaluating deployment opportunities across different business functions, understanding critical success factors that differentiate successful implementations from failed pilots, and anticipating organizational changes required for effective integration. The conclusions provide direction for bridging the persistent gap between AI technological capabilities and practical business outcomes, while outlining promising avenues for future research into economic impact longer-term socioeconomic consequences of widespread AI adoption on workforce composition and organizational structures.

W7225060782.abstract: Machine Learning, Deep Learning, and Robotics are revolutionizing the landscape of intelligent information management and decision support, connecting data processing, predictive analysis, and autonomous action. This review discusses the conceptual background, technological architectures, and application areas of integrated intelligent systems. It brings together the latest advances in machine learning, deep learning, robotic perception, autonomous control, reinforcement learning, digital twins, edge AI, federated learning and human-in-the-loop decision support. The review also compares the machine learning, deep learning, robotics, and integrated approaches in terms of accuracy, scalability, adaptability, computational efficiency, explainability, and real-time decision making. These technologies are increasingly becoming relevant in the healthcare sector, in manufacturing, in supply chains, in the finance sector, in cybersecurity, in smart cities, in agriculture, and in environmental monitoring. While significant strides have been made, there are still numerous challenges to address, such as data quality, privacy, security, interoperability, computational complexity, transparency, and trust. Multimodal intelligence, foundation models, Distributed learning, and Self-learning robotics are expected to become increasingly common in future intelligent systems. In summary, learning, reasoning, and robotic execution, when integrated, provide a strong basis for trustworthy, adaptive, explainable and human-centric decision support in real-world complex environments and retain the effectiveness of human involvement in the decision process and the responsibility of system governance.

W7225086287.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) are increasingly used for tasks involving structured knowledge, yet their outputs often fail to adhere to the semantic, logical, structural, and provenance constraints defined by formal ontologies. While existing benchmarks focus on factual accuracy or general reasoning, ontology-oriented tools primarily evaluate ontology quality rather than model behaviour, leaving a gap in assessing how LLMs interact with symbolic knowledge structures. This paper introduces a unified framework for evaluating LLMs in relation to ontologies. The framework integrates multi-domain grounding, multi-task prompting, and five complementary dimensions of correctness: semantic fidelity, logical consistency, ontology faithfulness, provenance support, and structural coherence. Additionally, a taxonomy of ontology-grounded errors provides a systematic basis for analysing characteristic failure modes, such as semantic drift and hierarchy misplacement. Synthetic scenarios illustrate how tasks, metrics, and error detection interact procedurally, while benchmark-inspired examples demonstrate how ontology-grounded deviations manifest across diverse knowledge domains. The proposed structure offers a reproducible and ontology-compliant foundation for analysing LLM behaviour in semantically constrained environments and lays the groundwork for future ontology-aware benchmarks and intelligent knowledge engineering systems.

W7225102908.abstract: Coordinating populations of LLM-powered agents toward cooperative outcomes while preserving ethical guarantees is a central challenge for intelligent generative systems deployed in adversarial environments. We present a framework in which a central LLM coordinator compiles natural-language directives into structured influence policies that are filtered by a constitutional governance layer before delivery to a heterogeneous population of grounded agents. Each agent follows a hybrid decision model that combines game-theoretic base probabilities with LLM-evaluated narrative shifts attenuated by per-agent resistance, and is instantiated from one of six personality archetypes (pragmatist, idealist, skeptic, conformist, strategist, opportunist) that reflect the diversity of real-world decision-maker profiles. Four experiments on a Barabási–Albert scale-free network of 30 agents over 50 time steps, powered by Llama-3.3-70B-Instruct, demonstrate that constitutional governance reliably preserves ethical coordination quality under full adversarial pressure: governed agents achieve an Ethical Cooperation Score (ECS) of 0.176 versus an unconstrained baseline of ECS=0, enforced through hard constraints on factual claim integrity (1.000 vs. 0.000). We identify an autonomy paradox in which unconstrained agents exhibit higher measured autonomy (0.856 vs. 0.728) by resisting manipulation more forcefully; yet, their overall coordination quality collapses through integrity failure, showing that agent-level resistance alone cannot substitute for system-level governance. Critically, the ECS governance advantage grows monotonically with mean resistance (+0.174 at R=0.10 to +0.183 at R=0.70), revealing that governance filtering and agent autonomy are complementary rather than redundant mechanisms in LLM-mediated coordination. Multi-seed bootstrap validation (Cohen’s d=8.68 for ECS) and an extended robustness sweep across three network topologies and five LLM backbones confirm that the governance advantage is structural rather than backbone- or seed-specific. These findings carry direct implications for the design of trustworthy LLM-driven autonomous agents and workflow automation systems operating in complex, adversarially contested environments.

W7225122817.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is changing the conduct of science. Models predict protein structures and propose materials, generate hypotheses, design and execute experiments, and increasingly assist in writing the papers that report the results. This paper examines the effect of these developments on the scientific method, drawing on the philosophy of science, the research-integrity and reproducibility literatures, and recent work on AI-driven discovery across the natural, engineering and social sciences. It distinguishes three functions of science that AI affects differently: discovery, the identification of what is the case; explanation, the account of why it is the case; and reproducibility, the possibility of independent confirmation. The paper argues that AI substantially accelerates discovery, threatens explanation, because predictive success without mechanistic understanding is now attainable at scale, and complicates reproducibility, since AI-driven results depend on models, data and computing conditions that are seldom reported in full or readily reproduced. It sets out a corresponding division of epistemic labour between human scientists and AI systems and a set of reporting and verification standards for AI-assisted research, and it considers the particular implications for scientific institutions in Africa, which may gain access to discovery capacity previously beyond their means while facing acute risks of irreproducibility and of dependence upon others. It argues that these three effects pull in different directions rather than reinforcing one another, so that the governance of AI-assisted research cannot treat acceleration, understanding and confirmation as a single problem. The paper sets out propositions on where predictive models may stand in for mechanistic explanation and where they may not, and proposes that African scientific institutions adopt explicit standards for the reporting and verification of AI-assisted results as a condition of building research capacity that is independent rather than dependent.

W7225143295.abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) is a machine learning paradigm in which an agent learns a decision-making policy by interacting with an environment, guided by a scalar reward rather than explicit supervision. Supervised and unsupervised learning have become indispensable tools in high-energy physics (HEP), but they learn from fixed datasets, whereas many HEP tasks are closed-loop decisions: the data an algorithm observes depend on its choices, the feedback is sparse or delayed, and the objective is often measured on a real machine or in a stochastic simulation, not by a differentiable model. This survey reviews the application of RL to such tasks: accelerator control and feedback, data quality monitoring, jet grooming, clustering, and representation, charged particle tracking, beyond-the-Standard-Model (BSM) and string model building, detector design, trigger control, analysis, and formal quantum field theory computation. It provides a self-contained introduction to the underlying RL methods, from model-free and model-based to multi-agent, offline, inverse, and bandit approaches, reviews each domain against its traditional methods, and summarizes the head-to-head comparisons. The applications range from policies deployed on real accelerators and evaluated on recorded collision data to exploratory studies in formal theory. RL is most advantageous for repeated tasks with a fast simulator, decisions inside fast control loops, operation under faults and corrupted measurements, physics-based rewards in place of labels, and sequential discrete constructions with a reusable policy, while Bayesian optimization, genetic algorithms, and differentiable methods remain competitive elsewhere. We conclude with the open challenges that recur across domains, including reward design, sim-to-real transfer, safety, the lack of shared benchmarks, and the statistical validity of policy-driven decisions.

W7225174315.abstract: Small language models (SLMs) offer an alternative to large general-purpose models when latency, privacy, cost and constrained computing resources are important. Agentic artificial intelligence extends language-model applications beyond single-turn generation by coordinating planning, tool use, memory, verification and iterative actions. This paper proposes a modular framework that combines an instruction-tuned SLM with a task planner, retrieval and memory services, permissioned tools, an execution monitor and human approval gates. The architecture is intended for bounded tasks such as document retrieval, scheduling and structured information processing. A risk-aware operating cycle and a reproducible evaluation protocol are specified, covering task completion, answer grounding, latency, resource consumption, security and human oversight. The contribution is an integrated reference design and test methodology, not a claim of a trained new model or an experimentally validated agent. The analysis identifies deployment trade-offs, failure modes and research directions for dependable SLM-based agents.

W7225306775.abstract: Cancer stem cells (CSCs) are a major contributor to therapeutic resistance, tumour recurrence, and disease progression because of their self-renewal capacity, phenotypic plasticity, immune evasion, and ability to persist after treatment. Chimeric antigen receptor (CAR)-based immunotherapy has transformed the treatment of several hematological malignancies, but effective targeting of CSC-driven disease, especially solid tumour, remains challenging. Antigen heterogeneity and loss, CSC plasticity, CAR-cell dysfunction, metabolic constraints, and an immunosuppressive tumour microenvironment (TME) can limit long-term therapeutic responses. CSC-associated antigens such as CD133, CD44, EpCAM, HER2, CSPG4, ALDH, and EGFRvIII have been investigated as CAR targets, although their heterogeneous and context-dependent expression raises important concerns regarding CSC specificity and on-target/off-tumour toxicity. Artificial intelligence (AI) and computational approaches provide opportunities to integrate genomic, transcriptomic, proteomic, spatial, and clinical data for CSC-associated antigen discovery, biomarker identification, CAR design, patient stratification, and toxicity prediction. However, the evidence supporting these applications varies considerably, ranging from computational and preclinical studies to retrospective clinical modelling, while prospective clinical validation of AI-guided CSC-targeted CAR therapy remains limited. Similarly, next-generation platforms, including CAR-natural killer (CAR-NK) cells, CAR-macrophages (CAR-M), gamma-delta CAR-T cells, and CAR-invariant natural killer T (CAR-iNKT) cells, remain at different stages of translational development. This review critically examines CSC biology, mechanisms of resistance to CAR-based therapy, emerging CAR platforms, and the potential role of AI in precision immunogenetics. Particular emphasis is placed on differentiating CSC-intrinsic, CAR-cell-intrinsic, and TME-mediated resistance and on defining the evidence maturity of AI applications. Finally, current challenges in data availability, tumour heterogeneity, model bias, external validation, interpretability, safety, and prospective clinical translation are discussed, together with priorities for developing clinically validated AI-enabled CSC-targeted CAR therapies.
